samples.text:
The pie chart shows the reasons for forest loss in the world between 2001 and 2020, and the bar chart shows how much forest was lost in four regions in the same period.

Overall, the main causes was agriculture, logging and wildfire, and South America lost the most forest.

In the pie chart, commodity agriculture was the biggest cause with 27%. Forestry, which means logging, was nearly the same with 26%. Wildfire and shifting agriculture had the same percentage, 23% each. Urban expansion was very small cause, only 1%. If we add the two kinds of agriculture together, it is half of the forest loss.

In the bar chart, South America lost 89 million hectares of forest, which was the highest. Africa was the second with 76 million hectares and Asia lost 72 million hectares, so they was quite similar. North America lost the least forest, 58 million hectares, but it is still a big number.

To conclude, forests were lost for many reasons and in all of the four regions, but the most loss was in South America.
samples.why: Overview present but general · key figures accurate and both visuals covered · simple linking and some informal phrasing (it is still a big number) · errors in agreement, articles and word form.

samples.text:
The pie chart illustrates the main causes of forest loss worldwide from 2001 to 2020, and the bar chart compares the area of forest lost in four regions over the same two decades.

Overall, forest loss was caused mainly by four factors of roughly equal importance, while urban expansion played only a minimal role. Among the regions, South America lost the largest area of forest and North America the smallest.

According to the pie chart, commodity agriculture was responsible for the largest share of forest loss, at 27%, closely followed by forestry, or logging, at 26%. Wildfires and shifting agriculture each accounted for 23%, which mean that agriculture of both types together caused half of all forest loss. By contrast, urban expansion was responsible for just 1%.

Turning to the regional data, South America lost 89 million hectares of forest during this period, the highest figure among the four regions. Africa and Asia experienced similar losses, of 76 and 72 million hectares respectively. North America lost the least, 58 million hectares, although this was still around two thirds of the South American figure.
samples.why: Clear overview of causes and regions · key features highlighted, with sensible grouping of agricultural causes · good cohesion · some less common vocabulary (minimal, responsible for) · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
The pie chart breaks down the causes of global forest loss between 2001 and 2020, while the bar chart compares the area of forest lost in four regions over the same period.

Forest loss resulted from four main drivers of broadly similar significance, with urban expansion a negligible factor. Regionally, South America suffered the greatest losses, although all four regions lost substantial areas of forest.

Commodity agriculture was the single largest cause, accounting for 27% of forest loss, marginally ahead of forestry and logging at 26%. Wildfire and shifting agriculture were each responsible for 23%, so that the two forms of agriculture combined were behind exactly half of all losses. Urban expansion, by comparison, contributed a mere 1%.

South America lost 89 million hectares of forest, the largest area of the four regions. Africa and Asia recorded comparable losses of 76 and 72 million hectares respectively, while North America lost the least, at 58 million hectares. Even so, the gap between the highest and lowest figures was relatively modest, at 31 million hectares, and together the four regions lost almost 300 million hectares of forest over the two decades.
samples.why: Well-judged overview · data grouped insightfully (combined agriculture, regional total) with accurate derived figures · seamless cohesion · precise vocabulary (drivers, negligible, comparable) · varied, error-free structures.
